---
title: "Quiz: finding spots"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Spots are Gaussians of known width σ (in pixels); "noise" is white noise of standard deviation $\sigma_n$ unless stated.

---

**Q1.** What is the output of spot detection, and how does it differ from the output of a segmentation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of what you would hand to a tracking program.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A **list of points**: a position $(x, y)$ per spot, usually with a brightness and a score (and later an uncertainty). A segmentation gives a mask or label image, i.e. which pixels belong to an object. Spots are only a few pixels wide and their shape is known (the PSF), so their extent carries no information; their position does.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why do spots in a fluorescence image all have about the same size, unlike the blobs of the [edges day](../scale-space/lec.qmd)?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the image of an object much smaller than the resolution?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The labelled objects (single molecules, small vesicles) are much smaller than the resolution, so each is imaged as the PSF: the same shape, only the brightness differs. So the filter can be tuned to one σ (the PSF width in pixels) instead of searching over scales.
:::

---

**Q3.** A spot has peak amplitude 30 above the background and the noise has standard deviation 10. What is its single-pixel SNR? About how much better is the matched filter for σ = 2 pixels?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The matched-filter SNR is $A\sqrt{\pi\sigma^2}/\sigma_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Single pixel: $30/10 = 3$. Matched filter: $3\sqrt{\pi \cdot 4} = 3 \cdot 3.54 \approx 10.6$, about 3.5 times better: the filter collects the signal of the roughly $\pi\sigma^2 \approx 13$ pixels the spot covers.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does smoothing with a Gaussian much **wider** than the spot make detection worse, not better?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the wide filter average outside the spot?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Outside the spot there is only noise (and background). A wide filter averages in many pixels that carry no signal: the response to the spot falls (most of the filter weight now sits where the spot is dark) faster than the noise does. The optimum is a filter of the spot's own width; it also keeps neighbouring spots apart.
:::

---

**Q5.** A Gaussian filter works well on one image and gives hundreds of false spots on the next, which has a bright patch of uneven illumination. Explain, and name two fixes.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a kernel with positive weights summing to 1 do to a constant?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The Gaussian passes the background unchanged, so on the bright patch every noise maximum is "bright" and passes a global threshold. Fixes: a **zero-mean** filter (spot template minus its mean, LoG or DoG: a constant gives zero response), subtracting a strongly blurred copy or a white top-hat before filtering, or the à trous product (the background ends up in the last smooth level).
:::

---

**Q6.** In the à trous detector, why **multiply** the thresholded levels $w_2$ and $w_3$ instead of adding them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the product if one factor is zero?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A product is non-zero only where **every** level passed its threshold. A spot of 1–2 px gives a positive response in both $w_2$ and $w_3$ at the same place; a noise fluctuation rarely does (it lives mostly in $w_1$ and is not coherent across scales). So the product keeps spots and removes most of the noise; a sum would keep anything that is strong at one scale.
:::

---

**Q7.** Two real spots can be as close as 4 pixels. Which window radius $r$ for the local maxima would you choose, and what goes wrong with $r = 1$ and with $r = 8$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The window is $(2r+1) \times (2r+1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$r = 3$ (a 7 × 7 window): a spot 4 px away is outside the window, so both spots stay candidates. With $r = 1$, noise ripples on one spot can each be a maximum of their 3 × 3 window: several candidates per spot. With $r = 8$, a dim spot within 8 px of a brighter one is never the maximum of its window: it is lost.
:::

---

**Q8.** Name three other places in the course where "keep a local maximum, suppress its neighbours" appears, and what plays the role of the window there.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Edges, blobs, voting, registration, neural network detectors.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Canny's non-maximum suppression (the two neighbours across the edge), blob detection in scale space (26 neighbours in $(x, y, \sigma)$), Hough accumulators (a window in parameter space), the peak of a phase-correlation surface, greedy NMS of boxes in deep-learning detectors (boxes with a large overlap).
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show with Cauchy–Schwarz that no filter $\mathbf w$ gives a higher SNR for the spot $A\mathbf p$ in white noise than $\mathbf w = \mathbf p$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
SNR $= A\,\mathbf w^\top\mathbf p/(\sigma_n\|\mathbf w\|)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$|\mathbf w^\top\mathbf p| \le \|\mathbf w\|\,\|\mathbf p\|$, so SNR $\le A\|\mathbf p\|/\sigma_n$, with equality exactly when $\mathbf w$ is a positive multiple of $\mathbf p$. Scaling $\mathbf w$ changes signal and noise equally, so only the direction matters.
:::
